## Definition

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_S\in\mathbb R$ be a nonempty finite pooled collection,
where $S\ge1$. Give each observation its average rank $r_i$ among all $S$
values; equal values receive the average of the ranks they occupy. Let $\Phi$
be the standard-normal CDF from [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]. Define
the Blom normal score

$$z_i=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{r_i-3/8}{S+1/4}\right).$$

The standard-normal CDF is continuous, strictly increasing, and has limits $0$
and $1$ at the two infinities by
[[lem-standard-normal-cdf-is-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]]. Since
$1\le r_i\le S$, the fraction lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, so its inverse
is a unique finite real number. This convention averages ties before applying
the score transform.

## Definition

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_S\in\mathbb R$ with $S\ge1$, and let
$x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(S)}$ be these values in nondecreasing order,
retaining multiplicities. For $0<u\le1$, the **left empirical $u$-quantile** is

$$Q_S(u):=x_{(\lceil Su\rceil)}.$$

Thus ties are retained, and the empirical CDF is
$F_S(t)=S^{-1}\#\{i:x_i\le t\}$. In particular, for $0<u<1$,
$Q_S(u)=\inf\{t:F_S(t)\ge u\}$. No interpolation between adjacent order
statistics is performed.

## Definition

Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ and put
$f(x)=1/(\pi(1+x^2))$. Define the **standard Cauchy law** to be the measure
$\mu_C=f\,d\lambda$ given by [[def-measure-with-density]]. The proof below
verifies that this measure has total mass one, so it is a probability law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R$ and the function
$f(x)=1/(\pi(1+x^2))$.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, inherited by the Borel-to-Lebesgue
and continuous-function measurability interfaces. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] On $\mathbb R$, Lebesgue measure is the restriction of Lebesgue outer
measure to the Lebesgue sigma-algebra; under Countable Choice every Borel set
is Lebesgue measurable.
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]

[F2] The function $f$ is continuous because polynomials, constants, scalar
multiples, and quotients with nonzero denominator preserve continuity; a
continuous function $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is Borel measurable under Countable
Choice. [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]
[[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]

[F3] A nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable density $f$ defines the measure
$f\,d\lambda(A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda$.
[[def-measure-with-density]]

[F4] A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is bounded and
Riemann integrable; under Countable Choice its Lebesgue integral there equals
its Riemann integral.
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]
[[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]

[F5] $\arctan x=\int_0^x(1+t^2)^{-1}\,dt$ for every real $x$, and oriented integrals are additive over adjacent intervals.
[[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]

[F6] The principal inverse tangent is a strictly increasing bijection from
$\mathbb R$ onto $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.
[[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]

[F7] Tangent is odd on its domain, so its inverse on the symmetric principal
interval is odd. [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]

[F8] If nonnegative measurable functions $g_n$ increase pointwise to $g$, then
$\int g_n\,d\lambda\uparrow\int g\,d\lambda$.
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F9] A measure is a probability measure when its total mass is one. [[def-probability-measure]] Also, $\pi>0$. [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]

[F10] For every real $r$ there is a natural $n$ with $n>r$. [[thm-of-archimedean]]

[F11] If $E$ is measurable and $g$ is nonnegative measurable, then $g\mathbf1_E$ is measurable. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $1+x^2\ge1$ and $\pi>0$ by [F9], the denominator in $f$ is positive. By [F2], $f$ is continuous and Borel measurable; [A1] and [F1] make it Lebesgue measurable. It is nonnegative, so [F3] defines the measure $\mu_C=f\,d\lambda$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F9, given]

1.2 For each integer $n\ge1$, $f$ is continuous on $[-n,n]$, so [F4] permits evaluation of its Lebesgue integral by the Riemann integral. By [F5] and the evenness of $(1+x^2)^{-1}$, $\mu_C([-n,n])=\pi^{-1}\int_{-n}^n(1+x^2)^{-1}dx =(\arctan n-\arctan(-n))/\pi=2\arctan(n)/\pi$; the last equality follows from [F7]. [A1, F4, F5, F7, given]

1.3 The sequence $\arctan(n)$ is increasing and bounded above by $\pi/2$ by [F6]. For any $0<\varepsilon<\pi$, put $u=\pi/2-\varepsilon$ and $r=\tan u$. By [F10], all sufficiently large natural $n$ satisfy $n>r$, so strict increase and the inverse identity in [F6] give $\pi/2-\varepsilon=u<\arctan(n)<\pi/2$. This is the epsilon definition of $\arctan(n)\to\pi/2$. [given, F6, F10, algebra]

2.1 The interval $[-n,n]$ is Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable by [F1]; [F11] makes $f\mathbf1_{[-n,n]}$ measurable. These nonnegative functions increase pointwise to $f$. By [F8], step 1.2, and step 1.3, $\mu_C(\mathbb R)=\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\lambda =\lim_{n\to\infty}\mu_C([-n,n])=1$. Thus $\mu_C$ is a probability measure by [F9]. [F1, F8, F9, F11, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Definition

Let $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary real process in the sense of
[[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]], and suppose
$0<\sigma_h^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_0)<\infty$ using
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For $k\ge1$, put

$$\rho_h(k):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)}{\sigma_h^2}.$$

If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\rho_h(k)|<\infty$ and
$\tau_h:=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_h(k)>0$, define the theoretical
**functional-specific effective sample size** for $n$ draws by
$\operatorname{ESS}_h(n):=n/\tau_h$. Here $Y_n=h(X_n)$ is the scalar
functional whose Monte Carlo average is being assessed. When a central limit
theorem for that average has asymptotic variance
$\sigma_h^2\tau_h$, this definition is the iid sample size with the same
asymptotic variance. It does not assert that such a central limit theorem holds.
If the covariance series is not absolutely summable or $\tau_h\le0$, this
definition does not assign a finite positive effective sample size.

## Definition

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ scalar chains $x_{m,1},\ldots,x_{m,L}$ of equal length
$L\ge4$.

1. Let $N=\lfloor L/2\rfloor$. Replace each original chain by two chains: its
   first $N$ observations and its last $N$ observations. If $L$ is odd, discard
   the middle observation. There are now $M'=2M$ chains of length $N\ge2$.
2. For each split chain $j$, compute its mean $\bar x_j$ and sample variance
   $s_j^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(x_{j,i}-\bar x_j)^2$. Put
   $\bar x_{\cdot}=M'^{-1}\sum_j\bar x_j$,
   $W=M'^{-1}\sum_j s_j^2$, and
   $B=N(M'-1)^{-1}\sum_j(\bar x_j-\bar x_{\cdot})^2$.
3. If $W=0$, return **not estimable**. Otherwise return
   $$\widehat R_{\rm split}=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V^+}{W}},\qquad \widehat V^+=\frac{N-1}{N}W+\frac{B}{N}.$$

This finite-sample formula is not clamped below at $1$; identical split-chain
means can therefore give a value slightly below $1$. Its interpretation as a
convergence diagnostic requires more than the arithmetic procedure itself.

## Definition

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ scalar chains $y_{m,1},\ldots,y_{m,N}$ of equal length
$N\ge2$. The procedure estimates the functional-specific quantity in
[[def-functional-specific-effective-sample-size]] from the observed arrays; it
does not test whether the chains are stationary or satisfy a central limit
theorem.

1. Compute the chain means $\bar y_m$, sample variances
   $s_m^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_{m,i}-\bar y_m)^2$, their average
   $W=M^{-1}\sum_m s_m^2$, the grand mean
   $\bar y_{\cdot}=M^{-1}\sum_m\bar y_m$, the between-chain term
   $B=N(M-1)^{-1}\sum_m(\bar y_m-\bar y_{\cdot})^2$, and
   $\widehat V^+=(N-1)W/N+B/N$.
2. If any chain has zero sample variance, or $\widehat V^+=0$, return
   **not estimable**. For $0\le t<N$, compute the biased autocovariance
   $\widehat\gamma_{t,m}=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N-t}(y_{m,i}-\bar y_m)(y_{m,i+t}-\bar y_m)$
   and $\widehat r_{t,m}=\widehat\gamma_{t,m}/\widehat\gamma_{0,m}$.
   Combine chains by
   $$\widehat\rho_t=1-\frac{W-M^{-1}\sum_m s_m^2\widehat r_{t,m}}{\widehat V^+}.$$
3. For $k=0,\ldots,\lfloor(N-2)/2\rfloor$, form
   $P_k=\widehat\rho_{2k}+\widehat\rho_{2k+1}$. If $P_0\le0$, return
   **not estimable**. Let $K$ be the largest $k$ for which
   $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ are all positive; $K=0$ if $P_1\le0$. Set
   $\widetilde P_k=\min_{0\le j\le k}P_j$ for $0\le k\le K$ and
   $\widehat\tau=-1+2\sum_{k=0}^K\widetilde P_k$.
4. If $\widehat\tau\le0$, return **not estimable**. Otherwise return
   $\widehat{\operatorname{ESS}}=MN/\widehat\tau$.

Negative serial correlation can make this estimate exceed the number $MN$ of
stored draws. The output is an estimator, not a guarantee about the target law.

## Definition

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ equal-length scalar chains with at least four observations
each. Let $S$ be the total number of pooled draws.

1. Apply [[def-blom-rank-normalization-for-pooled-draws]] to all pooled draws,
   split the transformed chains as in
   [[alg-split-rhat-from-multiple-chains]], and calculate the split statistic
   $R_z$ on the transformed values.
2. Compute the pooled median $m$ by sorting all $S$ draws and averaging the two
   central order statistics when $S$ is even (using the central order statistic
   when $S$ is odd). Fold each original draw to $|x_{m,n}-m|$, apply the same
   pooled rank-normal transformation to these folded values, split each folded
   chain, and calculate the split statistic $R_f$.
3. If either split calculation is not estimable, return **not estimable**.
   Otherwise return $\widehat R=\max\{R_z,R_f\}$.

The rank-normalized component addresses location and trend differences in a
finite output array; folding the absolute deviations makes the reported maximum
sensitive to scale differences as well. It is a diagnostic procedure, not a
proof of stationarity or convergence.

## Definition

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ equal-length scalar chains. Pool all draws and apply
[[def-blom-rank-normalization-for-pooled-draws]]. Apply
[[alg-multichain-effective-sample-size]] to the resulting $M$ transformed
chains. The output is the **bulk effective sample size** for this procedure.

Rank normalization makes this diagnostic finite for every finite real-valued
draw array, including arrays whose target distribution might have infinite mean
or variance. It is an efficiency diagnostic for the transformed values and is
not, by itself, a Monte Carlo standard error for the original posterior mean.

## Definition

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ equal-length chains of scalar draws. Pool the draws and
calculate $q_{.05}=Q_S(.05)$ and $q_{.95}=Q_S(.95)$ using
[[def-empirical-left-quantile-for-finite-draws]]. For each
$p\in\{.05,.95\}$, form the bounded indicator chains
$I^{(p)}_{m,n}=\mathbf1\{x_{m,n}\le q_p\}$, pool their values, apply
[[def-blom-rank-normalization-for-pooled-draws]], and apply
[[alg-multichain-effective-sample-size]] to the transformed indicator chains.

If either indicator ESS is not estimable, return **not estimable**. Otherwise
return the minimum of the two values. This is a tail-focused efficiency
diagnostic; it does not establish that a quantile estimate has a specified
error bound.

## Definition

**Inputs:** $M\ge2$ equal-length scalar chains, a quantile level $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
and the fixed levels $u_-=.16$ and $u_+=.84$ used for a one-standard-error
approximation.

1. Pool the draws and compute $\widehat q_\alpha=Q_S(\alpha)$ by
   [[def-empirical-left-quantile-for-finite-draws]]. Form the indicator chains
   $I_{m,n}=\mathbf1\{x_{m,n}\le\widehat q_\alpha\}$, Blom-normalize their
   pooled values by [[def-blom-rank-normalization-for-pooled-draws]], and
   compute $E_\alpha$ with [[alg-multichain-effective-sample-size]]. If the
   indicator chains are constant or $E_\alpha$ is not estimable, return
   **not estimable**.
2. Set $a=E_\alpha\alpha+1$ and
   $b=E_\alpha(1-\alpha)+1$. For $u\in(0,1)$, define the lower Beta quantile
   $Q_{a,b}(u)=\inf\{t\in[0,1]:F_{a,b}(t)\ge u\}$, where
   $F_{a,b}(t)=\operatorname{Beta}(a,b)((0,t])$ and
   [[def-beta-distribution]] supplies the probability measure. Let
   $v_-=Q_{a,b}(u_-)$ and $v_+=Q_{a,b}(u_+)$.
3. Return the approximate Monte Carlo error interval
   $[Q_S(v_-),Q_S(v_+)]$ and the estimate
   $$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat q_\alpha)=\frac{Q_S(v_+)-Q_S(v_-)}2.$$

All Beta shape parameters are positive because $E_\alpha>0$ and
$0<\alpha<1$. This is a finite-run approximation, not a theorem that the
interval has a prescribed coverage probability. Its statistical interpretation
requires conditions for the relevant quantile and indicator-chain limit
behavior; none are asserted here.

## Example

Let $E=\{0,1\}$, let $\pi$ be uniform, and take the transition matrix
$P(0,0)=P(1,1)=.9$ and $P(0,1)=P(1,0)=.1$. Start the chain in $\pi$. For
$Y_n=2X_n-1$, the lag-$k$ autocorrelation is $\rho(k)=.8^k$. The theoretical
functional-specific ESS per $n$ transitions is $n/9$. If only every tenth
state is retained, its lag-one correlation is $.8^{10}\approx.1074$, but its
ESS under the same transition budget is approximately $.0806n$, below the
unthinned $.1111n$.

[F1] A transition matrix has probability rows and defines its one-step

[F2] Invariance means $\pi P=\pi$ on every measurable set.
[[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]

[F3] The process stationarity convention is strict invariance of all finite
dimensional laws under common time shifts.
[[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]

[F4] $\operatorname{ESS}_h(n)=n/(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_h(k))$ when the
autocorrelation sum is absolutely convergent and positive.
[[def-functional-specific-effective-sample-size]]

[F5] A time-homogeneous chain has one-step conditional transition law given by
its probability kernel relative to the stated filtration.
[[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]]

[F6] Covariance and variance use centered second moments.
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

**Given:** The Markov chain and observable in the Example.

1.1 Each row of $P$ is nonnegative and sums to one. The uniform law is invariant because each column also sums to one, so $\pi P=\pi$ by [F1] and [F2]. By [F5], the transition rule is time homogeneous. Repeated use of the Markov property gives, for times $n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and states $x_1,\ldots,x_r$, the path probability $\pi(x_1)\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}P^{n_{j+1}-n_j}(x_j,x_{j+1})$: the first marginal is $\pi$ because $\pi P=\pi$, and each later gap uses the corresponding matrix iterate. 1.2 Under $\pi$, $\mathbb E[Y_n]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=1$ by [F6]. ## Remarks

Thinning can still be useful when storing a draw or evaluating a particular
functional is costly. Owen's discussion in §11.13 treats those storage and
computation tradeoffs; the calculation above compares effective sample size
under a fixed number of transitions when all states can be retained.

## Example

This finite funnel-shaped model has state space $E=\{n\}\cup B$ with the
discrete sigma-algebra, where $n=(0,0)$ is the narrow state and
$B=\{(v,x):v\in\{1,2,3,4\},\ x\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}\}$ is the broad region.
Let $\pi(n)=1/2$ and give each state in $B$ mass $1/32$. Let $K$ fix $n$ and
cycle through the 16 states of $B$ in lexicographic order, beginning at
$(1,-2)$. Let $\Pi$ be the independent-refresh kernel
$\Pi(x,\{y\})=\pi(y)$ and put $P=.99K+.01\Pi$. Start four chains at $(1,-2)$
and use independent transition randomness. On an event of probability
$.99^{124}$, all 124 transitions use $K$. Every chain then misses the narrow
state, even though it has target mass $1/2$. On that event the rank-normalized
folded split $\widehat R$ for each coordinate is $\sqrt{15/16}<1$.

## Example

The standard Cauchy law has density $f(x)=1/(\pi(1+x^2))$ by [[def-standard-cauchy-law]]. Its second moment is
infinite, so the population variance used to interpret an unranked variance
diagnostic does not exist. Separately, take two finite chains of length eight:

$$x_1=(-1,-1,1,1,-1,-1,1,1),\qquad x_2=(1,1,3,3,1,1,3,3).$$

The raw split statistic and the rank-normalized split statistic on these
location-shifted arrays are both $\sqrt{7/4}$; the folded component is

distinct from the paper's replicated Cauchy simulations, which are empirical

## Definition

**Inputs:** Real outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, an integer $n\ge2$, and an integer batch size $b$ with $1\le b<n$. For an MCMC run, $y_i=f(X_i)$ for the chosen real-valued observable $f$.

**Outputs:** The sample mean $\bar y_n$, the overlapping-batch-means estimate $\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}$, and its estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

1. Compute the sample mean
$$\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.$$

2. For each starting index $j=1,\ldots,n-b+1$, compute the overlapping batch mean
$$\bar y_j(b)=\frac1b\sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}y_i.$$

3. Return the overlapping-batch-means variance estimate
$$\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}=\frac{nb}{(n-b)(n-b+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b+1}\bigl(\bar y_j(b)-\bar y_n\bigr)^2.$$

4. Return the estimated Monte Carlo standard error
$$\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar y_n)=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{OBM}}/n}.$$

All sums are finite, the denominator is positive because $b<n$, and the variance estimate is nonnegative. The procedure always returns a number for the stated finite input. It does not by itself assert a CLT or consistency; consistency requires the hypotheses of the overlapping-batch-means theorem.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a
$\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to $\phi$ ([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]) with invariant probability
$\pi$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary
$P$-chain whose canonical left shift preserves its path law and whose
shift-invariant measurable events have probability zero or one. We take the
initial law to be $\pi$, which implies stationarity by
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]. Let
$f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$
be Borel with $\pi(f)=0$. Define
$\sigma_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$
only when the covariance series is absolutely convergent and the CLT is
established, as in
[[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Each of the following six conditions is sufficient for absolute convergence
of the covariance series and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2):$$

1. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>1$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   and $f$ is essentially bounded under $\pi$ (there is $B<\infty$ with
   $|f|\le B$ $\pi$-almost everywhere).
2. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>0$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some $\delta>0$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and
   $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some
   $\delta>0$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and
   $\pi\bigl(f^2\log^+|f|\bigr)<\infty$, with
   $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]), reversible with respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense ([[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]), and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

In case 4, the displayed logarithmic moment implies $f\in L^2(\pi)$: on $\{|f|\le e\}$ one has $f^2\le e^2$, and on $\{|f|>e\}$ one has $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$.

When $\sigma_f^2=0$, the zero-variance lemma
[[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate
normal limit from absolute covariance summability. Finite variance of $f$
alone is not one of the sufficient conditions.

## Statement

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$, the jointly
measurable probability-kernel family $(P_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$, common
invariant probability $\pi$, and adaptive process $(X_n,\Gamma_n)$ satisfy
[[def-diminishing-adaptation]]. Fix an initial law $\mu_0$ for
$(X_0,\Gamma_0)$; a fixed initial pair is the Dirac-law special case. If
diminishing adaptation holds under this law and either of the following
conditions holds, then
$$\lVert\mathcal L_{\mu_0}(X_n)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\longrightarrow0.$$

1. **Simultaneous uniform ergodicity:** for every $\epsilon>0$ there is an
   integer $N(\epsilon)\ge1$ such that
   $$\sup_{x\in\mathsf X,\,\gamma\in\Gamma}\lVert P_\gamma^{N(\epsilon)}(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon.$$

2. **Containment:** for every $\epsilon,\delta>0$ there is an integer $N$
   such that
   $$\mathbb P_{\mu_0}\!\left(M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N\right)\ge1-\delta\quad\text{for every }n\ge0,$$
   where $M_\epsilon$ is the fixed-kernel convergence time from
   [[def-adaptive-mcmc-containment]].

The conclusion is convergence of the one-time marginal distributions. It does
not itself assert a strong law, a central limit theorem, or convergence of
sample averages.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A common target probability $\pi$, probability kernels
$(P_\gamma)$ satisfying $\pi P_\gamma=\pi$, an initial law $\mu_0$, and an
adaptive process whose conditional transition at time $n$ is
$P_{\Gamma_n}(X_n,\cdot)$.

[F1] [[def-diminishing-adaptation]]: $D_n=\sup_x\lVert
P_{\Gamma_{n+1}}(x,\cdot)-P_{\Gamma_n}(x,\cdot)\rVert_{\rm TV}$ is
measurable, lies in $[0,1]$, and tends to zero in probability.

[F2] [[def-adaptive-mcmc-containment]]: $M_\epsilon(x,\gamma)$ is the first
positive iterate at which the fixed kernel $P_\gamma$ is within $\epsilon$ of
$\pi$, and containment gives a uniform-in-$n$ probability bound for it.

[F3] [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]:
$\pi P_\gamma=\pi$ for every fixed $\gamma$.

[F4] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]: total variation
is the supremum of setwise probability differences.

[F5] [[lem-total-variation-coupling-and-kernel-contraction]]: Markov kernels
contract total variation; hence
$\lVert P_\gamma^{m+1}(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le
\lVert P_\gamma^m(x,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}$.

[F6] [[lem-adaptive-mcmc-block-perturbation-bound]]: over a fixed block of
$N$ steps, the adaptive marginal differs from the mixture obtained by freezing
$\Gamma_n$ by at most $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}\mathbb E D_{n+j}$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and facts [F1]–[F6]. All probabilities and
expectations below use the specified initial law $\mu_0$.

1.1 Since $0\le D_n\le1$ and $D_n\to0$ in probability, for each fixed $j\ge0$ we have $\mathbb E D_{n+j}\to0$: for any $t>0$, $\mathbb E D_{n+j}\le t+\mathbb P(D_{n+j}>t)$; first let $n\to\infty$ and then $t\downarrow0$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Assume simultaneous uniform ergodicity and fix a desired tolerance $\eta>0$. Choose $N=N(\eta/2)$ as in alternative 1. For the frozen mixture $Q_{n,N}$ from [F6], every state and parameter has $\lVert P_{\Gamma_n}^{N}(X_n,\cdot)-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\eta/2$, so convexity of the setwise supremum gives $\lVert Q_{n,N}-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\eta/2$. [F3, F4, F6, given]

1.3 Now assume containment. Fix $\eta>0$, take $\epsilon=\delta=\eta/3$, and choose $N$ from alternative 2. On the event $M_\epsilon(X_n,\Gamma_n)\le N$, the definition gives an iterate $m\le N$ within $\epsilon$ of $\pi$; [F5] propagates this bound to the $N$th iterate. On the complementary event total variation is at most one. Therefore the frozen mixture satisfies $\lVert Q_{n,N}-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\epsilon+\delta=2\eta/3$ for every $n$. [F2, F4, F5, given]

2.1 For this fixed $N$, [F6] and step 1.1 imply $\lVert\mathcal L(X_{n+N})-Q_{n,N}\rVert_{\rm TV}\to0$, since its upper bound is a finite sum of expectations tending to zero. The triangle inequality and step 1.2 yield $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\lVert\mathcal L(X_{n+N})-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\eta/2$. As $n+N$ ranges over all sufficiently large times and $\eta>0$ is arbitrary, the asserted convergence follows in alternative 1. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The same fixed-block bound [F6] tends to zero by step 1.1. The triangle inequality gives $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\lVert\mathcal L(X_{n+N})-\pi\rVert_{\rm TV}\le2\eta/3<\eta$. Again $N$ is fixed and $\eta$ is arbitrary, proving the asserted convergence in alternative 2. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. For $\alpha,\beta>0$, the **Beta distribution** $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ is the probability measure on $(0,1)$ with density
$$f_{\alpha,\beta}(p)=\frac{p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. The finite positive normalization follows from
[[lem-beta-density-normalization]]. The open interval is the parameter domain;
no endpoint atoms are included.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\alpha,\beta>0$, the nonnegative function
$p\mapsto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ and
$$\int_{(0,1)}p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\,d\lambda_1(p) =B(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)} \in(0,\infty).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and positive real numbers $\alpha,\beta$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom assumed by the bounded-Riemann-to-Lebesgue integral theorem. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The real Beta function is the improper integral of $p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ on $(0,1)$. [[def-real-beta-integral]].

[F2] For positive $\alpha,\beta$, $B(\alpha,\beta)=\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)$. [[thm-real-beta-gamma-identity]].

[F3] The Euler Gamma integral is finite and strictly positive for every positive argument. [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

[F4] A bounded Riemann-integrable function on a closed bounded interval is Lebesgue measurable and has the same Lebesgue and Riemann integrals under Countable Choice. [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]].

[F5] Continuous functions on a closed bounded interval are bounded and Riemann integrable. [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]].

[F6] Increasing limits of nonnegative measurable functions have integrals equal to the increasing limit of their integrals. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]].

[F7] The improper Beta integral converges for positive parameters. [[thm-real-beta-integral-convergence]].

[F8] Positive real powers are continuous on $(0,\infty)$. [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]].

[F9] The integral is with respect to the stated Lebesgue measure. [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and $\alpha,\beta>0$.

1.1 By [F8], $f(p)=p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is continuous and hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ with the measure in [F9]. For each integer $m\ge2$, its restriction to $[1/m,1-1/m]$ is continuous, hence bounded and Riemann integrable by [F5], and [F4] identifies its Lebesgue integral with its Riemann integral. The indicators of these intervals increase pointwise to one, so the truncated functions increase to $f$. [A1, F4, F5, F8, F9, construct]

2.1 By [F6], the Lebesgue integral of $f$ is the limit of the truncated integrals from step 1.1. The same truncations define the improper integral in [F1], which converges by [F7]; therefore the limit is $B(\alpha,\beta)$. [step 1.1, F1, F6, F7]

3.1 The identity in [F2] and positivity and finiteness in [F3] show that $B(\alpha,\beta)$ is finite and strictly positive. This proves the displayed Lebesgue integral identity and its endpoint bounds. [step 2.1, F2, F3] ∎
